title: Arguing Over Standardized Tests
script: Aisyah: [thoughtful] I just got my results back, and honestly, I don't think a three-hour multiple-choice exam captures anything meaningful about what I actually know.
Bagas: I sympathize, but isn't the alternative even messier? At least a standardized test can be compared fairly across thousands of applicants.
Aisyah: [carefully] Fair to whom, though? Someone who's been coached since childhood has an obvious advantage over someone sitting for the first time with no preparation.
Bagas: That's a legitimate point, and I won't pretend the playing field is level, because it clearly isn't.
Aisyah: [reflective] So why do universities keep relying on a system they privately admit is flawed?
Bagas: Partly inertia, I'd guess, and partly because the alternatives, portfolios, interviews, essays, are harder to standardize and easier to game in different ways.
Aisyah: [honestly] I hadn't considered that essays could be gamed too, though I suppose wealthier applicants can afford better editors.
Bagas: Exactly, which suggests the problem isn't really the test itself, it's that advantage finds a way through whichever door is left open.
Aisyah: [gently] Maybe what bothers me most is being reduced to a single number, as if three hours could summarize years of effort.
Bagas: I understand that, though for what it's worth, most admissions officers claim the score is only ever one factor among several.
Aisyah: [calmly] Claim being the operative word. It's hard not to suspect that, when applications pile up, the number becomes a convenient shortcut.
Bagas: Probably true under pressure, yes, though I'd rather universities be transparent about that shortcut than pretend it doesn't happen.
Aisyah: [encouraging] Agreed. If the number's going to matter this much, the least they owe us is honesty about how much it actually matters.
Bagas: On that, at least, we're in complete agreement.
